utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning counsel, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner and Daryl Mundis. We are assisted today by our intern, Lisa Hartog, and our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for Defence counsel who are all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic counsel, Stephane Bourgon co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, Judge Swart has nothing on his screen, although I could lend him my screen. We will continue nevertheless. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the two accused, General Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Kubura. I would like to greet the witness, the judge, as well as everyone else in and around the courtroom. We will continue with the hearing of this witness today. Yesterday the cross-examination was being conducted and I will now give the floor to the Prosecution since the cross-examination has not yet been completed. Mr. Neuner, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ahmetovic. If disputes arose in 1993 about the status of a person under investigation, whether he was a civilian or a soldier at the time of committing the crime, which judge or which Chamber was in a position to make a determination on the status of a suspect or an accused, of status as a civilian or as a member of a military unit?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigative judge or the person filing the criminal report against such a person. It was his duty at the very beginning when filing the criminal report to make the situation clear, to determine whether it was a civilian or a member of the military. This would be done by requiring a certificate from the Ministry of Defence to see whether such an individual had been mobilised as a member of the military and see whether it was perhaps a civilian. This is how his status would be determined. If his status was not determined in the course of the investigation, objections were raised to the situation, to the circumstances, then the Chamber of the regional military court consisting of three Judges would decide on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You just mentioned certificates. You mentioned certificates of the Ministry of Defence. Could also 3rd Corps itself or 3rd Corps units issue such certificates that the person concerned was a member of its units?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. Every military unit had its own records, and when examining the records, having examined the records, they could issue a certificate stating whether someone was a member of their unit or not. But this then concerned only that unit. But the Ministry of Defence had a record about the greatest number of individuals mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What value would such a certificate have in the litigation of the issue whether the person's status -- has the status of a civilian or military person? What value would it have?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We treated this as evidence, and it was on that basis that we decided on our competence. We decided whether a military court or a civilian court was competent to try such a person. So until doubt was cast on the validity of a certificate, such certificates were accepted because the competent organ or unit had issued the certificate in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You were yesterday shown a judgement by the Defence, and this is contained in the Defence binder, section 4, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is a judgement of the district military court in Zenica dating 3 June 1993. Section 4, the judgement section, in there tab 2. This is a judgement against accused persons from the 303rd Mountain Brigade, and the issue of certificates is mentioned in the section Statement of Reason. On the B/C/S version, that's page 6 of the judgement, the fourth paragraph. In the English version, it's also page 6 but the third paragraph, and I'm referring to the first sentence here. Can you find this? The first sentence I'm referring to states, and I quote: "All the accused are undoubtedly members of the RBiH army 303rd Zenica Mountain Brigade, which was corroborated by a certificate issued by the command on 3 May 1993." Does this portion of the judgement confirm what you just said a moment ago about the weight of these certificates?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Let me move on. If I show you a report about the work accomplished by the Zenica District Military Court from October 1993 until March 1994, would you be in a position to comment on the basis of this document on the work of your own court?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have a look at the document, and I will then answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the Prosecution exhibits, tab 3. It's Exhibit DH275. Document relating to the report on the District Military Court in Zenica, dating 8 March 1994. And on the last page you see it's signed by the president of this court, Mr. Muhamed Colakovic. You had a document signed by him yesterday in front of you. It relates to the period from 1 October 1993 until 28 February 1994, and it states at the beginning of the document: "308 requests for investigations and 258 indictments have been received by the District Military Court." If you look on the first page, on the fifth paragraph, please, it states: "The situation in Zenica municipality as at 28 February 1994." Do you find this, please? Do you find this?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Following that there are numerous categories of crimes listed which were either investigated by the Zenica District Military Court or tried. Judge Ahmetovic, I'm asking you to review quickly the categories of crimes listed and tell the Court whether in the period October 1993 until the end of February 1994 any war crimes, according to chapter 16 of the SFRY penal code were dealt with by the District Military Court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this report only the basis of the heading, the Zenica District Military Court. I can recognise it on the basis of the stamp of the Zenica District Military Court, and on the basis of the sit of my former president, Muhamed Colakovic. I really couldn't comment on these figures contained in this report. I accept them as valid figures. As far as these crimes listed, I believe it only concerns a report to the municipality of Zenica and to the Ministry of Defence, a report that concerns individuals who were mobilised into the ranks of the ABiH through the Ministry of Defence in Zenica municipality. So the Ministry of Defence has records on the number of individuals who abandoned the ranks of the ABiH. This is the crime of leave and desertion from the armed forces referred to in Article 217 of the Criminal Code of the socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. This shows that some individuals who were mobilised wilfully deserted military units, and they were no longer considered as members of the military or as members of the ABiH, and as such that the disposal of the Ministry of Defence -- rather, the ministry of defence in the municipality of Zenica can try to determine their location to mobilise them again. The failure to respond to the call-up and evasion of military service which is Article 214, this is also a familiar article from the criminal law and was frequently invoked in our Court. And this concerns the fact that civilians to whom call-up papers were sent either refused to receive the call-up papers and refused to be mobilised or they received the call-up papers but they failed to report to the military unit they were supposed to report to. Similarly, these individuals had committed a crime and criminal proceedings were instituted against them. And this report was forwarded to the Ministry of Defence in the Zenica municipality in order to inform them of the fact that it was necessary for them to find those individuals again and send them call-up papers again. They were also informed the fact that criminal proceedings had been instituted for the crime committed, and that concerns the other crimes listed as well. As to your question about whether individuals were processed for war crimes, tried for war crimes, I really couldn't say. I don't have the record or the records from the district court before me, but yesterday after the hearing I remembered that towards the end of September or beginning of October 2003, some -- some workers, some employees from The Hague Tribunal scanned the records of the Zenica District Court. I think you have these records, and I think that on the basis of these records you can determine whether any proceedings were instituted for war crimes during that period. It's very difficult for me to answer such a question now, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on the document just in front of you, can you maybe have a short look and find out whether in this document there are any investigations or judgements listed in relation to war crimes? This was my only question, whether within this particular document you find any record about it.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having had a quick look at this document, I don't see that the Zenica District Military Court instituted any investigations into war crimes. They didn't investigate anyone, members of the military, civilians, members of the ABiH, or members of the HVO or some other military formation, or perhaps members of the Republika Srpska army at the time. So I can't see that the District Court dealt with war crimes during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look now at the last page of this document, in the B/C/S version it's the second last paragraph. In the English version it's the last paragraph. The president of the Zenica military court states here, and I quote: "There is also a problem with some ABiH units when this comes to serving summons to their members. They refused to receive them, although the law says that summons for members of the ABiH can only be served through their units. These problems badly affect and slow down the work of this court." Mr. Ahmetovic, having worked in the relevant time period at the District Military Court in Zenica, what is meant exactly here?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the president of my court wanted to say in this sentence at the time, but I think that this is a quote from the Law on Criminal Procedure. I believe that my president was quoting the law from the Law on Criminal Procedure. It's the duty of courts and prosecution -- and the prosecution to send call-up papers through commands and their units. We weren't in a position to send such call-up papers to the address of such individuals, so perhaps some colleagues had problems which they mentioned to the president of the court. Believe me, I didn't come across such problems in the course of my work. Military units sent court papers and individuals responded. When they didn't respond, when this wasn't possible, an order was issued to have these people brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So with call-up papers you're referring to a summon to appear in a proceeding or as witness for investigation? Please just clarify.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an investigative judge, and the call-up papers I sent were sent to suspects and witnesses in investigation. My colleague, Mladen Veseljak sent summons for a trial, and then there were accused, witnesses, injured parties, and others who participated in the proceedings. So summons were issued.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, summons, not call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you could turn to the Defence finder again. It is section 1 this time, tab 5. It's DH1560, a document dated from 28 December 1993. A decision to open investigation into a case involving grave robbery. I think the document is in B/C/S only.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I ask you to look at the last page first. It's page 2, I think. Your name and, I think, your initials are mentioned there on the last page. It is correct?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this document well, and I remember the individuals into whom investigations were opened by virtue of my decision dated the 28th of December, 1993. These aren't my initials here. My full name and surname is contained here, and my signature on a decision whereby I opened an investigation into Osmancevic Alem and Pezer Sefik. As far as I remember, it was believed that they had committed robbery according to the Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a document that states that criminal proceedings were instituted against certain individuals. The decision on carrying out an investigation from the investigative judge is the document that institutes proceedings. If you don't have such a document, criminal proceedings can't be instituted against an accused or against a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The second person mentioned under 2 on the first page is Sefik Pezer, and I think it states in the last line of this paragraph relating to the paragraph preceded by number 2 that he was a member of the military police of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade since 7 July -- since July 1993. And I believe at the time you wrote this report, Mr. Sefik Pezer was still at large. So he wasn't in the -- in anybody's custody. My question is: Did you subsequently to this document order the arrest of the second suspect at large, Sefik Pezer?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there is an awkward translation or whether you have failed to understand the Law on Criminal Procedure. I can't issue an order for arrest. The investigative judge acts on the basis of a request launch an investigation which is submitted by the prosecutor's office. In this case by the military prosecutor's office in Zenica. As far as I can remember in that request for an investigation, no suggestion had been made to detain this person. If I decided to detain this person, I needed to draft a decision stating that he should be detained and not to issue an order for his arrest. As far as I can remember, this person responded to the summons. He wasn't fleeing. He was accessible. My court could find him, and the state organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina could gain access to him. There is no order for arrest. There's only a decision on detention, which is based on the suggestion of the prosecutor's office. It's true that the investigative judge, on the basis of the case file, on the basis of the situation, could state that someone should be detained even if the prosecutor had not made such a suggestion. This could be done if there were legal reasons pursuant to Article 191, paragraph 1, and 191, paragraph 2. Items 1, 2, 3 and 4 on the Law on Criminal Procedure. And this was applied at the time by the Zenica District Military Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer himself was a member of the military police. Is this a rare case that, so to speak, a member of the organs who are supposed to enforce law and order did engage in potential criminal conduct, or was it occurring from time to time during your work in late 1993/1994 that you had suspect among the military police?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that that was the case only during that period. Even today if you have information that a policeman committed a crime, this will make anyone normal feel that he should have doubts about the work of such a person as a policeman. And on the basis of this information and this investigation, I believe that we should all draw the conclusion, and we can draw this conclusion, we should draw the conclusion that no one at the time was immune to criminal prosecution, even if the person in question was a military policeman of the 7th Muslim Brigade in Zenica. And if he had committed a crime, he should be held accountable. And I must say that I appreciate the fact that the commander of the 7th Muslim tried to deal with their very close associates. This shows how serious the 7th Muslim command was in the sense that they were trying to form or establish a real military unit. As far as I can remember, Mr. Pezer was sentenced to two and a half years in prison in our court, and this is not a light sentence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to criminal reports. You mentioned yesterday several times these criminal reports, and these documents constitute usually the first written description of an incident. And I take it from your words usually these documents are produced before a formal investigation has been started; correct?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course you're right, and I will repeat what I have already said. An investigation or the Prosecution of someone commences once the investigative judge has taken a decision on carrying out an investigation. Everything else is done before of the investigation. You gather evidence on a crime committed. The criminal report, which charges an individual with a certain crime, is part of the factual description of the way in which the crime committed. And it also contains the legal qualification. It states the kind of crime that is concerned, and it refers to the article according to which the individual a charged with a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in fact, these criminal reports, they are the important tool to trigger subsequent investigations?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible to qualify this as important or not important. It is simply envisaged as a document pursuant to which the competent prosecutor decides whether to instigate proceedings against somebody or not. In addition to the criminal report, the competent prosecution bodies could also issue a report on the crime. This is a different document based on which the prosecutor also could decide whether to Prosecution doubt the person or not. According to the law, this is provided for, and this just could not be avoided. So it is not the matter of this being important or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to clarify what you just have said, is it possible for a district military prosecutor to request an opening of investigation without a criminal report received?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure, this situation is envisaged, because it says in the law that every person is authorised to report a crime, and this includes the prosecution. If he receives rumours that a crime has been committed and if he is aware who the perpetrator might be, he can instigate proceedings against that person regardless of the subsequent stage in the proceeding. That is, regardless of whether the criminal report will be filed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you please look in the prosecution bundle at tab 4. This is DH155-2. It's a report by the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion about criminal reports filed, and this document dates the 28th of March, 1994, so shortly after the document DH275, which you have seen a moment ago. And the subject of this document is the number of criminal reports filed. And it is mentioned on the first page that 377 criminal reports relating to 824 perpetrators have been filed. This is letter A on page 1. And the time period is 14 September 1992 until 1st of March, 1994. So roughly a 17-month time period. Do you find letter A? If I take these 377 criminal reports -- and I'm interested to determine how many criminal reports per month have been filed. So if I take these 377 criminal reports and divide them by 17, I get a figure of 22.17, meaning in an average per month 22 criminal reports have been filed by the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion. Do you find that having worked as an investigative judge that the filing of an average of 22 criminal reports per month by the 3rd Corps military police over a 17-month period constitutes a small, an average, or a great number of criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, this is a document of the battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps, which was sent to the BiH army 3rd Corps. So this document has nothing whatsoever to do with the District Court of Zenica or me as an investigative judge. As I sit here, I cannot comment upon all of these figures which are listed here. They may be correct. They may not -- they don't have to be correct, but this is not a document that I can comment upon. It is maybe Mr. Mujezinovic who could provide you with a comment because he draft this had document and he had the most insight into those documents. As to whether this is a lot to have the military police battalion filing 22 reports, I don't know. They filed reports on anything that might have happened on the ground where crimes were committed. They reported on all the events, and they processed them. In addition to them, criminal reports could be filed by citizens, by the Ministry of Defence, by military units or the command of the 3rd Corps. Any institution could file such reports, because it was a legal obligation set out by the Law on Criminal Procedure in which it says that whoever found out about a crime was duty-bound to report such a crime. In other words, would I not dwell upon this document any longer. I would like to refer you to Mr. Mujezinovic with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm just interested in one small section of this document. You stated you prefer not to talk too much in detail about it, but I think this is an abstract or a section which can be generalised. It's under letter C, and it is just mentioned against whom the criminal reports were filed. You find section C? There are six categories of persons against whom the reports were filed, and I'm just listing them: Members of the eye BiH; second, members of the HVO against civilians --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President. The witness said that he could not comment upon this document, and on our list of witnesses, we have Mr. Mujezinovic who drafted this document. I believe that it would be only fair and appropriate for the Prosecutor to leave these questions for our witness Mujezinovic, who is to come here very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, have you heard the remark by the Defence? They believe that the author of this document, who is about to be called, is better placed to comment upon this document, because this witness says that he cannot comment upon this document as regards the figures in the document that you may ask him to comment upon. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I turn to my last subject, then. The legal requirements for criminal reports, how they should be drafted. Can you please look at tab number 7 of the Prosecution exhibits. DH115, decree having the force of law on the district military prosecutor's office, dating 13th of August, 1992. And in Article 6 of this decree, it states the following: "In discharging the function of criminal prosecution, the district military prosecutor shall cooperate with the authorities obliged under the law to detect and report criminal offences falling under the jurisdiction of military courts for which prosecution is undertaken ex officio." So the authorities obliged under law to detect and report criminal offences. You mentioned already. Is this the military police, the military security also, and civilians? Can you please clarify? What are the authorities obliged under the law to report criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decree law on military prosecutors' offices that I have before me is a bylaw. Above it is the Law on Criminal Procedure which is very clear when it comes to the criminal prosecution of certain persons. I've already said that according to that law, according to the umbrella law, the highest law on the criminal proceeding -- proceedings, every person, every citizen, every military or civilian institution is obliged to report a crime at the moment they learnt about that crime. Article 6 is of a lesser scope, and it arises from this decree law. However, the Law on Criminal Procedure provides anybody with a much lesser scope for proceedings in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With regard to the filing of criminal reports by the military security, can you please look under tab 8 of your bundle. This is P244. At section 41, and the first sentence. It states here relating to the military security service, and I quote: "On the basis of the information --" okay. Just waiting. Do you have it? I quote again: "On the basis of the information gathered, officers of the military security service in the command of the brigade or a corresponding or higher-ranking office near the military security service shall submit a criminal report to the competent military prosecutor's office in cases when it is necessary to carry out certain investigative actions immediately, an authorised officer of the military security shall immediately inform the competent --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when you're reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I repeat that question again: "In cases when it is necessary to carry out certain investigative actions immediately, an authorised officer of the military security service shall immediately inform the competent military prosecutor and, when necessary, also the investigating judge of the military court."

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not manage to find this. You were rather fast. I heard your question, however. This those how military institutions and personnel acted, and this is even a more narrow document. This is -- these are rules of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina where it says that personnel of the military security have to detect the criminal and report to the prosecutor's office. In case they found the perpetrator on the scene, then they had to report that to the military investigative judge or the judge on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you couldn't find section 41. Have you found it now, please? I'm just referring to the third or last -- no, you haven't found it. Section 41 in tab 8. Or Article 41. Have you found it now? Thank you. I'm referring to the last sentence of Article 41 which talks about the requirements of a criminal report. "Together," it states here, and I quote: "Together with the criminal report, objects, sketches, photographs, reports, files on measures and actions undertaken, official notes, statements, and other materials which may be helpful for the successful conduct of the trial are also submitted." The criminal reports which you received in late 1993, early 1994, did they contain the objects mentioned here in section 41?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal reports were sent to the competent military prosecutor's office in Zenica, and if they decided to prosecute such person or persons, they would submit a request for investigation against such person or persons, and this request, together with all the evidence, would be submitted to me as an investigative judge. In the last sentence of paragraph 41, it says that together with the criminal report, objects, sketches, photographs, reports, files on measures and actions undertaken, official notes, statements and other materials which may be helpful for the successful conduct of the trial are also submitted. This is, I believe, just a copy -- this sentence that I have just read out has been copied from the Law on Criminal Procedure. Everybody, including the military security body, was duty bound to submit to the investigative judge all the evidence that they came across in their effort to detect the crime and the perpetrators thereof. It doesn't necessarily mean that every criminal report had to contain all of these objects, sketches, photos, and so on and so forth. There are places where this is not done. There are situations when this is not done. It all depends on the structure of the crime that was committed. For example, crimes pursuant to Article 217 of the penal code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is wilful abandonment of a military unit, you don't need any evidence. You don't need a sketch or a photo. However, when it comes to a robbery, to a murder, aggravated robbery, a traffic accident, you have to have photos accompanying your report. You have to have a sketch of the site where the crime happened, and all the other evidence pursuant to which you will be able to tell that a certain person committed a crime. Basically, it all depends on the type of crime. But in a nutshell, I would like to conclude by saying that these items were submitted. They were submitted. They have to be. In addition to that, the question is how cable is the military security body of collecting certain evidence and to which extent they can do that. Sometimes evidence is destroyed before it could be found. Sometimes it is hidden or is not accessible for one reason or another. Therefore, the prosecution bodies are not in a position to deliver that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We looked at the rules for the military security service. I'm asking you now to look at the rules for the military police. This is tab 5 of your binder. P328. First of all, if you look at section 67, in the second sentence --

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: 67. So in the second -- do you find it?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is in section 5. It's the page -- the page with the ERN number 02131207. Page 26, I think. Section 5 of the Prosecution bundle. Okay. You have it. Let me maybe, because we have lost some time, move on to the next page. It's section 69. Here you find the -- a description of what criminal reports should contain. Do you find this section 9? So I'm just stated a few examples. The criminal report should include basic details on the perpetrator, time and place of the commission of the crime, description of the offence. If you read quickly through this, did the criminal reports you received in late 1993, early 1994, did they contain these details, the criminal reports received from the military police?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have only one question left relating to Vares. You testified yesterday about the jurisdiction of the Zenica District Military Court in relation to Vares. I just want to clarify. My question is: Did the Zenica District Military Court have jurisdiction over 3rd Corps units which were present in Vares area in late October and/or early November 1993?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution, at this point in time, has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Additional questions arising from the cross-examination or new questions authorised by the Chamber? The Defence, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ahmetovic. In response to my learned friend's questions, you said that a number of bodies were obliged to report crimes of which they had learnt or the perpetrators thereof. Is that what you said to my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The last few questions put to you by my learned friend were relative to the form of a criminal report. Before that, in response to one of the questions, you said that in addition to the criminal report, the competent prosecutor could learn about the crime or the perpetrator in other ways. Could you tell us, please, what other ways did you have in mind, the ways in which the competent prosecutor could be informed about grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed or that there is a person that could be suspected of having committed such a crime?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons who were duty-bound to inform the prosecutor of a certain crime, about which I testified, I said that the prosecutor himself could have heard rumours about a crime having been committed and the person who might have committed it, and based on that rumour, the prosecutor could prosecute that person. This is the most far-fetched way, but there were also other ways that the prosecutor could learn about a crime that may have been committed. This implies that the person who has information about a certain crime is duty-bound to report this crime. The person who does not have any information about a crime is not duty-bound to report anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All these ways of reporting to the prosecutor about the suspicion that a crime may have been committed, so all these ways, reports, official notes that you have just mentioned, and everything else, are all these legitimate ways to report the existence of such a suspicion to the competent prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what is envisaged by the law on criminal procedure, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were an investigative judge for a long time and you did not receive the original, the initial criminal report by which the prosecutor was informed directly at the time when the crime was reported, but when you received the -- all of the material from the prosecutor with a request to start an investigation, did you receive all the different forms of reporting, that is criminal reports, official notes? In practice, did all these documents reach you as possible ways of informing the prosecutor in a legal way that the crime may have been committed?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An excellent question. In my practice, I did not come across any other way of informing the prosecutor of a crime. The only form I encountered was a written criminal report or a -- or a report on the crime that was committed. I have not encountered any other way of informing the prosecutor of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To my learned friend's question about the commission of a crime and role of an investigative judge, you answered that as an investigative Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. judge who was sometimes on duty, you referred all the material and evidence collected in an investigation you referred to the prosecutor. My question to you is as follows: The investigative judge who collected material and who submit it had to the prosecutor, was he duty-bound to write a criminal report, or whether this material that the judge submitted to the prosecutor, did it constitute ample legal grounds for a prosecutor to start the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is very specific, but I must say that every time the duty judge goes out to investigate, he brings with him members of the team who are always members of the military or civilian police as prosecution bodies, and these prosecution bodies would all continue prosecuting such perpetrators. It was never the judge on duty who did that. The judge on duty would just form a team that he would take to the scene. He would take stock of the scene. He would take an official note or record of the investigation, and he would issue orders to the prosecuting bodies either in written or in oral form, and members of the team were duty-bound, and they always executed those orders, be it the collection of additional evidence, interviewing witnesses, securing the site of crime or similar things. In any case, the prosecution was taken over either by the civilian or the military police, which then filed a criminal report and informed the competent prosecutor thereof. The prosecutor, together with the duty -- judge on duty went to the crime scene. And I don't remember any situation during the war when I didn't have a prosecutor together with me. So if that is the case, nobody had to inform the prosecutor, because the prosecutor was already privy to the information about the crime, and he acted upon that in the way the law prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given as you have just said that the prosecutor was present at most of those on-site investigations, and you yourself and your colleagues also went to these on-site investigations, once you had provided him with all the material that you had gathered, who -- or, rather, which body was then authorised to request additional measures to be taken either by the court or by the police? Which is the body that was authorised to assess whether the material collected was sufficient in institute proceedings or not?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the duty judge had completed everything that had to be done at the on-site investigation, and after the members of the teams had provided written reports or material evidence, he would send to the competent prosecutor a record of the on-site investigation together with all the material evidence, physical evidence, official records, and certain statements. And from that point of time, the duty judge was no longer involved in the case. Up until the time that the competent prosecutor stated whether an individual be criminally prosecuted or not on the basis of that material. The only person who had the authority to decide whether criminal proceedings should be pursued was the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague mentioned the rules on military security. Please have a look under section 8 at page 11, item 41. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it says that if it is necessary to carry out certain investigations immediately, the competent officer from the military security service must inform the competent prosecutor and, if necessary, the judge of the military court. Can you tell me, how many times did you go to on-site investigations in one year, for example?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say how many times I went to on-site investigations. I know that decisions on appointing me as a duty judge were issued every fifth or seventh week, more or less. On the first week, and then the seventh week. On the first and then the fifth week I was the duty judge. This does not mean that it was always necessary to go to on-site investigations when I was the duty judge, so it's very difficult to say how frequently that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who informed you of the fact that there was an incident that should be investigated usually?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was usually informed by the military police of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, and very rarely I was informed by members of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the experience you had, could you tell me whether the security organ or the military police of the 3rd Corps performed its duties according to Article 41, item 2? Did they immediately inform the competent prosecutor or judge?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally members of the military police battalion, once they were informed of the fact that a crime had been committed, immediately informed the duty judge who would then decide whether it was necessary to go to the on-site investigation or not. And I must say that they were very responsible. The members of the military police battalion were very responsible, especially the criminal inspectors who had to perform those tasks in very difficult conditions. So to the extent it was possible, everything functioned in a satisfactory manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague showed you a report from the military police battalion. Let me just have a look. It's after number 4. DH155/2. Could you just have another look at the report that was shown to you. And my question is: Were individuals prosecuted for the crime committed or for the qualification of the crime?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals could never be prosecuted for the qualification of the crime. They could only be prosecuted for the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just want to object not to the question itself but to the fact that the question is based on the document DH155/2, because as the witness has pointed out, it's not a document from the Zenica District Military Court. It's from the Military Police Battalion, and the witness who has -- or the person who has signed this document, Zaim Mujezinovic is coming -- is your own witness coming in a few days. Therefore, I think it's more adequate to ask these questions at a later point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is making the same objection that you made earlier on. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 3, please. Although the question was quite different from the one put by the prosecutor, but never mind. I accept the fact that my learned friend raised the same objection. Under number 3, you will see document DH275, which is a report from the Zenica Military Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this document I'll put the same question to you. According to our criminal law, were individuals prosecuted for crime or for the qualification of the crime?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that it was just for the crime that they were prosecuted, not for the qualification of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague has shown you this document, DH275, and asked you whether there was an act, a chapter 16. Have a look at the crimes listed, murder, robbery, aggravated robbery, theft, et cetera, other forms of crimes. As a judge, are you aware of the fact that all these acts were described as possible war crimes against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. And I think that this is something that we discussed yesterday. Article 142 of the former criminal law of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and now it's Article 153 of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina provides this crime or provided the same description for the crime. All these crimes also constitute the crime of war crime again the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether in the case of all those crimes, the various forms of murder, violent behaviour, et cetera, for all these crimes were members of the ABiH prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, and this can be seen to a certain extent from the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the final assessment of those acts, who could provide the final assessment of those acts or the so-called legal qualification of the acts? Who provided the final legal qualification of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. I did so yesterday. The final legal qualification was provided in the court's judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my learned colleague, you mentioned numerous bodies that filed criminal reports with the prosecutor's office. As far as you knew, because you did not work in the prosecutor's office, but tell me on the basis of what you knew, because you were later forwarded the case as an investigative judge, tell me whether other military bodies and other military units, apart from the military police battalion, filed criminal reports against their own members.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. In addition to the military police battalion, criminal reports were also filed by the commands of all ABiH units in the 3rd Corps starting from the 303rd Mountain Brigade. This included the 7th Muslim and many other units that were in that area. They would file such criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague also asked you about the attitude of the court towards certificates issued by military units on the membership of certain individuals within those units, and you said that if the court didn't doubt the reliability of such certificates, these certificates were accepted as valid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the court ever verify whether someone was a member of a certain unit or not, even though no doubt had been cast on the document in question?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally the court only verified such matters if they did not have information on whether the individual concerned was really a member of the military or not. Very often, someone would decide about whether someone was a military member or not on the basis of his statement, bus there was no time to collect the certificate. In such situations, the investigating judge or the Presiding Judge would decide that the unit referred to by the suspect or the accused would be asked to provide a certificate stating whether the individual was a member of the unit or not. Very often individuals would be on record, but they had been at large for a long time. They weren't, in fact, members of those units. But someone had perhaps forgotten to delete them from the records. In such situations, one would try to locate the individual and then establish whether the individual was a member of the military unit or not. That is to say whether the individual was a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have anticipated my following question. With regard to the crimes mentioned by my colleague, you also mentioned the crime of leaving military units or failing to respond to the call-up, and you said that in such cases those individuals who failed to respond to the call-up to join units, or in the case of individuals who had wilfully abandoned units, in such cases they were no longer members of those units and they should be deleted from the record. Do you remember having said that in response to a question put to you by my colleague?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a judge in the District Military Court, did you ever come across situations in which you noticed that military units did not immediately delete the names of members from their records who had left the units in that way or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could answer this question in a number of ways. This all depended on the unit concerned. It varied from unit to unit. Some military units were highly organised, and they really took care in the personnel section to establish whether someone was really a member of the unit or not. And there were other units which failed to react in good time. It depended on the character of the people working in the personnel section. It depended on whether such individuals would be deleted from the records in time. So we really did sometimes receive certificates from a unit stating that an individual was a member of the unit and at the same time would have a criminal report stating that the individual had fled from the unit. That was a matter of disorganised records in the unit, and this would subsequently be corrected, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Given that situation, given what you have just mentioned, tell me whether the military police which detected perpetrators came across similar problems as far as complying with your orders is concerned or issuing summons, et cetera. And this is something that my colleague mentioned and something referred to in one of the reports.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your experience, the work of the military police battalion and military units, while you were a judge at the District Military Court, tell me, did the military police and other military bodies take all the necessary steps to resolve incidents they came across at that period of time and given the conditions that prevailed? Is that how you believe that they acted?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that the members of the military police battalion worked day and night insistently in order to detect the identity of the perpetrators of crimes. And this can be seen on the basis of the reports filed, on the basis of the individuals against whom reports were filed. The prosecutor noticed that in one case a report concerned a member of the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade. There were no exceptions. Anyone who committed a crime was reported. For example, I also had criminal reports against brigade commanders or the deputy brigade commander for security, logistics. There were criminal reports against battalion commanders, against deputy battalion commanders. So there were no exceptions. It was only important to determine whether someone had committed a crime or not, and no one was except from prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown the law on military police, and according to the document you were shown, it states that the military police must arrest and bring in individuals who were found to have committed a crime. Tell me, to what extent did the military police perform those duties when they detected an individual at the scene or when they managed to arrest an individual? Did the military police arrest such an individual and take such an individual to the investigative judge in accordance with the authority they had?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the responsibilities of members of the ABiH or, rather, of the 3rd Corps that was part of your responsibility, tell me whether you know to what extent the military units in the 3rd Corps had recourse to other measures. For example, disciplinary measures, disciplinary detention in relation to its members in order to discipline the army and prevent offences being committed. Do you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have information about this, and I can provide you with a very positive example. For example, the command of the 303rd Zenica Mountain Brigade filled its disciplinary detention units with its own members, members who were guilty of having committed offences. They were given 60 days -- up to 60 days in detention. So each unit acted in this manner in order to ensure that there was discipline in its units and in order to prevent crimes from being committed, in order to prevent misdemeanors from being committed, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank very much you, Judge. Yesterday, my learned colleague asked you about special military courts, and you mentioned the case of the Ilijas Brigade. You said that you had personal information about this example?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you say that there were similar decisions in other brigades' decisions that you were unfamiliar of, that you weren't aware of?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that there was a decree law which provided for all the unit commands to set up such special military courts, I believe that there may have been such situations in other units. I spoke only about this case that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to my learned friend's question about interviews and other technicalities, I would like to ask you something else about interviews. An investigative judge, when interviewing a suspect, and then the president of the Chamber when trying such suspect, do they inform the suspect that they have to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the provisions on the Law on Criminal Procedure that that we used, the investigative judge had to do that only with witnesses. A suspect or an accused was entitled to his defence, was entitled to answer questions, or could opt for silence. An accused or a suspect could not be warned about having to tell the truth. This did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a suspect or an accused did not tell the truth, were they punishable by law for perjury?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, my learned friend asked you something about the case of Dusina, and you said that you received that case later on according to the rules of the road, and that the case arrived from the military court in Travnik with a seat in Vitez, which is the body under the control of the HVO, and this arrived in your court via The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got hold of this case as an investigative judge, tell me, please, did you obtain all the evidence that the military district prosecutor had in 1993, and did you include all this evidence in the file?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about the Dusina case, I remember that I received this case in 2002, and in this case I found evidence that was collected in the course of 1994 and 1995, when the request for investigation had been filed. In other words, I believe that the security organs collected this evidence in the territory under the control of the HVO subsequently, and those were mostly statements of the persons who were involved immediately and directly in that event. Later on, I learned that these persons had fled to Busovaca, Kiseljak, or Vitez after the events. They were not accessible either to the military security of the 3rd Corps or the judiciary in Zenica or the law enforcement bodies in Zenica. Even if the proceedings had been instituted, these persons were not accessible. All the events, all the evidence of the crime was collected subsequently, in 1994 and 1995, and as far as I can remember, this event took place in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1993, your colleagues, judges on duty or investigative judges who went to the place where the bodies had been brought to, did they have an opportunity to take statements from the persons who gave their statements subsequently in the territory which was not under the control of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- during that period of time, I was the secretary of the district military prosecutor in Doboj seated in Tesanj. I don't have any immediate information about that. However, through the statements I took later on as an investigative judge in 2002 and 2003, I learned that all the participants in the event, and the victims of that event on that same day, the day before, the day later left the area and went to Busovaca, Vitez, Kiseljak, and other areas under the control of the HVO. My conclusion, thus, was that my colleagues who worked on that case were not in a position to find them, even if they looked for them. Whether they looked for them or not, I don't know. They can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be provided with DH258, 259, DH260, DH26 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We will do that after the break, because it is half past ten. We will now adjourn, and we will resume at five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume, and I will give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, Mr. President, I would like to repeat the number of the documents that should be given to the witness. I believe that they have already been prepared. Those are DH258, DH259, DH260, DH261, and DH156, document number 3. One of these documents, Mr. President, has been shown to a witness who testified under protective measures, and that is why I would ask questions arising from this document in a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session, I will give the floor to the Defence again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This concludes my re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now give the floor to Mr. Kubura's Defence team in case they have additional questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges now have some questions they would like to put to the witness. Judge Swart will start putting his questions to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Witness, I have a few questions to put to you on the basis of what you've said, and most of these questions have to do with existing legislation at the time you were an investigating judge in 1993. Yesterday, you made a distinction between, on the one hand, war crimes and, on the other hand, crimes committed in time of war, and what you said about the distinction corresponds, I believe, with what earlier in this week your former colleague Veseljak also told us. And I understood from your testimony and also the testimony of Veseljak that the category of crimes committed in time of war or when a war is imminent, danger of war is imminent was an important category for you and your colleagues. Now, I've looked at the Criminal Code for Bosnia that we have, and this is DH338 exhibit, but I cannot find a reference to a special category of crimes committed in time of war or in circumstances making it likely that a war is imminent. But this may be due to the fact that our copy of the Criminal Code dates from an earlier time. My first question to you is: Do you know or could you tell us when for the first time a Criminal Code was adopted in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as criminal legislation in Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, we should go back to the time when Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent and sovereign state recognised by a certain number of states in the world and recognised by the United Nations. In 1990 or, rather, in 1991, when Bosnia became independent, and on the 1st of March, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina officially declared its independence and became an independent state. Immediately after that event, in April 1992 war broke out. Aggression was committed against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and an imminent threat of war was declared, and war was declared in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that was in -- at the beginning of June 1992. At the time, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, finding itself in such a situation, issued decrees and adopted the laws of the former SFRY. And as of that time, these laws were called the laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but there is a document or, rather, a decree law in which these laws adopted as the laws of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that decree, the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina also adopted the criminal law and the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as of June or July 1992, this law became the official law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all regular and military courts in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina acted in accordance with that law. This legislation was in force in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina up until November 1998, when a new Law on Criminal Procedure was adopted and a new criminal law was adopted, but this time it didn't concern the territory of the entire republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a particular law and a particular law on criminal procedure for the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The second such law on the Law on Criminal Procedure and the criminal law -- a different law existed for the territory of the -- Republika Srpska. And the third type of law existed for the Brcko area. Later, when the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed, I think that was in March 2003, criminal law and the Law on Criminal Procedure was adopted for the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, but the federal law and the law for Republika Srpska and for the Brcko area continued to be valid. They are still valid today. They were valid up until the 1st of August, 2003, which is when a new criminal law and Law on Criminal Procedure was adopted. According to the new criminal law, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were no provisions for war crimes, but such provisions did exist in the state law applied by the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And we have all seen that that court will take over a number of cases from this court, and these cases will be dealt with in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this thorough overview of developments. So you said that in July 1992, a Bosnian Criminal Code was adopted, inspired maybe by the code of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you confirm that in November 1992, to be precise, on the 23rd of November, 1992, there was a decree law introducing a special category of crimes, crimes committed in time of war or imminent danger of war? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an occasion to see such a decree, but it is possible that exists. I did not have an opportunity to see it as a judge. I applied the Law on Criminal Procedure and the penal code that were in effect at that time and which had been adopted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the former state of Yugoslavia. It is possible that you're referring to the decree law by which the -- there are so many crimes for which the penalties were increased. For example, five years of imprisonment and for the majority of such crimes even death penalty was envisaged. For example, we had a situation during 1993 and 1994. The person who committed an aggravated theft, if it only implies one litre of oil which cost at that time 50 German marks in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for this person to be sentenced to death because the value of the stolen goods was more than 20 German marks. I believe that it was absurd at the time, but that's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That may -- that may very well be the decree I meant. I was referring to something that was said -- appeared from the testimony of your colleague -- your former colleague Veseljak, but I haven't seen the decree myself, so I'm just asking. I have another question not related to your testimony but to criminal law in general. Is this also the decree, can you tell us anything about it, on the basis of which the former chapter 16 of the Yugoslavian code on international crimes was made applicable for the Republic of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such decree. There was only a decree by which the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia was adopted as the Criminal Code of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in its chapter 16, there were provisions for such crimes. I believe that it was from Article 141 onwards, amongst which was the war crime against the civilian population that has been discussed in the course of the -- these two days. There was no special decree by which only these crimes were adopted. There was only a decree on the adoption of the entire laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much, because it is very hard for us to assess what is this legal situation in the legislative field without having all the documents. I would now like to ask you to turn again to an exhibit that has been discussed this morning and yesterday. That is number 3 of the Prosecutor's collection. It is DH275, a report that you have been commenting upon this morning already.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, this is the report of 8 March 1994, and the Exhibit number is DH275. If you look at the first page, you will note that at a certain point, an overview is given of specific cases. It starts with 27 individuals were convicted of the crime of unauthorised leave and desertion from the armed forces, and then you get other categories of crimes and other numbers. What is interesting for me at this moment is that this text says Article 217, 217, and punishable under Article 226 of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so the former code. So could you confirm that Article 26 of the former code of the former Yugoslavia is a provision on crimes in times of war or imminent danger of war? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this very well. This Article 226 is a provision which says that these are the grounds based on which only a military person who commits this crime from Article 217 can be punished only during the war or the imminent state of war. This means that if such a person is prosecuted pursuant to Rule 226 of this code, that the sentence is much more stringent than it would be in the case if the military person were prosecuted for the same crime in the time of peace, because this crime can be committed in the time of peace but also in the time of war and the imminent threat of war. Obviously, the -- it was absolutely justified to believe that it is very much harder to commit such a crime during the war and the consequences are much harsher during the war than in peace. A person abandons his unit in the peacetime, it is easy to find him. There are no consequences. However, if such a person abandons his unit in the times of war that means one rifle less for defence of the country. That's why the punishment is much harsher and that's why the Article 226 applies in these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I have been looking at a copy of Article 226 which I happened to find. Could you also confirm that this provision, Rule 226, as you said, is concerned about so-called crimes against public order. Specific category of crimes running from Article 198 to Article 225.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice, I did not have such cases. I didn't have anybody who was prosecuted for this type of crime on these grounds, and I believe that this is not provided for by the law. At least that's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm simply asking whether you remember whether this Article 226 of the code of the former republic was limited to crimes against the public order or had a more wider scope.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let's go back to the documents if -- you have before it. You see that list starts with a reference to Article 217 and then refers to Article 226 of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia. I'm inclined to think that Article 217 refers to the Bosnian code, and Article 226 to the code of the former Yugoslavia. Is that correct, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to say that you are wrong, although I'm younger and you are much more experienced. This is the same law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you are the expert and I am an outsider, so I accept what you are saying. Turn, then, to the next category. You see that some individuals were convicted for the crime of failure to respond to call-up and evasion of military service referred to in Article 214 and punishable under, again, Article 226 of the code of the former Yugoslavia. So there are two references to Article 226 of the code of the former Yugoslavia. And if you go down to the next category, other crimes against the armed forces, ten individuals have been convicted of other crimes against the armed forces, there is no reference any more to Article 226, and the same goes for the following categories. Can you follow me in what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So could you please explain to me why in the first two categories there is a reference to Article 226 and not in the other categories?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a legal solution. This Article 226 provides for more stringent punishment for a certain number of crimes, and it says expressly in this article what crimes can be punished more severely if it was committed during the war or the imminent threat of war. The article itself lists the crimes for which there may be more stringent penalties, and only in the cases of these crimes this can be done. This is what the law provides for, and this is what we applied. You have noticed very well that the following article, 214, is in connection with Article 226. These crimes may be committed only by the civilians, because these are persons which -- who were sent the call-up papers, and they refused to receive those call-up papers, or the person went into hiding in order to evade military service. And in this case -- in these cases, the military court was allowed to try civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you. If you look further and you come to murder, for instance. Article 36 of the code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There there is no reference to Article 226 of the code of the former Yugoslavia, although I could imagine that murder can also be committed in time of war, of course. So -- and the same goes for aggravated theft or for manslaughter. So could you please explain me the situation with regard to these three categories?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just the way it was done by the legislator in the former Republic of Yugoslavia who deemed that a certain number of crimes should be treated in one way in a times of peace and in a different way in times of war or imminent threat of war. Why murder, robbery, and aggravated robbery were listed under the category of crimes for -- which are equally treated in the war and in the time -- in the peace, I don't know. You know that murder is the same thing in the times of war as well as in the times of peace. The same goes for the robbery. I've already spoken about the crimes that fall under Article 226 of the Criminal Code. It is only up to the legislator to do that, and the judges and prosecutors could not react to that and say that, for example, in the times of war and imminent threat of war the Article 226 could be applied to other crimes because this was simply not envisaged by the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, you said yesterday, and your colleague, your former colleague, Veseljak, said, and I have no doubt to what you were saying, but you both said that a number of crimes committed in time of war could be more severely punished than when committed not in time of war. And your colleague -- your former colleague Veseljak also said this is for instance also the same for cases of aggravated theft. If you look at a documents, on the second page of the B/C/S version you see a reference to Article 148, paragraph 3, of the Bosnian code, and Article 148 is the provision on aggravated threat, isn't it? So I'm looking for a legal provision enabling you as a judge to impose heavier punishment than would be provided -- would be possible in time of peace. And maybe the secret is in paragraph 3 of -- paragraph 3 of Article 148. I've been looking to Article 148, but I have only two sections, 1 and 2, and number 3 is missing. So can you tell us what the third paragraph of Article 148 contains? Is that a paragraph that increases the punishment, the minimum and the maximum punishment, in time of war or is it something different?

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have the code before me, and I can't see the article. I believe that paragraph 3 was added subsequently when the existing law was amended. However, this paragraph 3 doesn't mean that this crime was committed during the times of war or imminent threat of war. I believe that it is only about the modus operandi, and this is all it contains. And why you believe that a heavier punishment could be attached to this crime has to do with a decree dated November 1993 by which the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina took a certain group of crimes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and placed it under a group of its own and increased penalties in view of the war and the imminent threat of war. Later on when peace came, these provisions were made null and void. It was only during the war and the imminent threat of war that we had this legal leap in the punishment policy. So it was increased by one step higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So may I conclude that there was a possibility to punish offences like aggravated threat or murder or manslaughter or other offences maybe with, let's say, a heavier penalty if committed in time of war but on the basis of some piece of legislation that I myself have not seen? Maybe the decree of November 1992 probably. I come to my last question on the -- this document. You said this morning that all these offences, murder, manslaughter, aggravated theft, et cetera, could also be considered to be crimes against the civilian population. And if you're using that expressions you imply may also be considered to be war crimes or other international crimes, because that is the formula used in chapter 16. What do you mean when you say this, all these offences listed here like murder, manslaughter, can also be considered to be crimes against the civilian population? I was not quite able to understand what you meant to say.

utterances.speaker: HILMO AHMETOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When answering that question put to me by the Defence, I provided a clear answer.
